claims.claim: Boats like the narrator's carry people and goods on the river
They travel by sail and oars
Smaller boats carried people and goods such as groceries.
Navigation on the river was done by sail and oars.

lines.en: Bread and water for Ti Joaquim's muleta; he won't leave the fishing ground. Boats like mine carry people and goods on the river, by sail and oars. Sheet in the sail, let's go.
lines.pt: Pão e água para a muleta do Ti Joaquim, que não sai do pesqueiro. Barcos como o meu levam gente e mercadoria pelo rio, à vela e a remos. Caça a vela, vamos.

claims.claim: Boats linked the banks of the Tejo
Boats carried people and cargo
Navigation was by sail and oars
River traffic linked the two banks of the Tejo, carrying goods and people.
Navigation on the Tejo was done by sail and oars.

lines.en: All aboard? The muleta won't wait. That's how the Tejo works: boats linking the banks, with people and cargo, by sail and oars. Sheet in a bit more.
lines.pt: Tudo a bordo? A muleta não espera. É assim que se anda no Tejo: barcos a ligar as margens, com gente e carga, à vela e a remos. Caça mais um pouco.

claims.claim: Any small river boat was once called a barca
Boats changed according to their work and route
The canoa is a distinct boat type from the bote
The term barca was long used for any small river-traffic or fishing boat on the Tagus.
Barcas came to diversify according to their functions and routes.
The canoa and the bote were distinct boats used for passenger transport.

lines.en: Once, any small river boat was called a barca. Then boats changed with their work and their route. This is a canoa. A canoa, not a bote. Hold that course.
lines.pt: Antigamente dizia-se barca a qualquer barco pequeno do rio. Depois os barcos foram mudando conforme o serviço e o caminho. Isto é uma canoa. Canoa, não bote. Mantém esse rumo.

claims.claim: Going upriver, entering creeks and fishing at sea each require different keel, bottom, mast and sail
The canoa carries people
The canoa carries small goods
Going upriver, entering creeks and fishing at sea required boats with differing keels, bottoms, masts and sails.
The canoa was used for passenger transport.
Smaller boats carried people and small goods.

lines.en: Going upriver, entering the creeks, fishing at sea: each job wants a different keel, bottom, mast and sail. My canoa carries people and small goods.
lines.pt: Subir o rio, entrar nos esteiros, pescar no mar: cada serviço pede outra quilha, outro fundo, outro mastro, outra vela. A minha canoa leva gente e coisas pequenas.

claims.claim: The river was the busiest road
Fragatas, varinos, faluas and catraios were distinct craft on the river
The river linked towns from Santarém to Cascais faster than any other way
The river was the busiest route of its time, with fragatas, varinos, faluas and catraios among its craft.
Boats linked towns between Santarém and Cascais faster than other means.

lines.en: The river is the busiest road there is. Fragatas, varinos, faluas, catraios... and don't mix them up. It links the towns from Santarém to Cascais faster than any other way.
lines.pt: O rio é a estrada mais movimentada que há. Fragatas, varinos, faluas, catraios... e não os confundas. Liga as terras de Santarém a Cascais mais depressa que qualquer outro caminho.

claims.claim: Acostar means to come alongside, with controlled speed

lines.en: Easy. Come alongside, don't ram her.

claims.claim: Coming alongside involves reducing speed
Muletas are fishing boats carrying fish
Fish is carried by water (river transport)
The fish is carried fresh and cannot wait
Bread is handed over in the exchange
The muleta is a fishing boat used on the Tagus.
Fish was carried by water.

lines.en: Well brought alongside. Hand over the bread and take the muleta's fish by water, fresh, it won't wait.
lines.pt: Bem acostado. Passa cá o pão e leva o peixe da muleta pela água, fresco, que não espera.

claims.claim: The fish is carried by water to the quay
The fish must arrive fresh

lines.en: Hm. You didn't hit me. That's something. The fish goes with you; get it to the quay fresh.
lines.pt: Hum. Não me bateste. Já é alguma coisa. O peixe vai contigo; que chegue fresco ao cais.

claims.claim: Muletas unload fish in great quantity at Lisbon
Old accounts tell of hundreds of boats unloading
A huge quantity of fish was unloaded at Lisbon by muletas, by hundreds of boats.

lines.en: There's Lisbon. Here the muletas unload fish in great quantity. The old accounts tell of hundreds of boats unloading.
lines.pt: Lá está Lisboa. Aqui as muletas descarregam peixe em quantidade. Os antigos contam de centenas de barcos a descarregar.

claims.claim: Muletas and caravels unloaded heaps of fish at Lisbon
This went on for a long time
Someone wrote it was hundreds of boats
Caravels and muletas unloaded a huge quantity of fish at Lisbon, by hundreds of boats, according to a written description.

lines.en: Look at the city. For a long time muletas and caravels have unloaded heaps of fish here. Someone once wrote it was hundreds of boats.
lines.pt: Olha a cidade. Há muito que muletas e caravelas despejam aqui montes de peixe. Houve quem escrevesse que eram centenas de barcos.

claims.claim: The Ribeira had loading and unloading all day
Everything was bought and sold at the Ribeira
Fish goes from Lisbon to Santarém by water
The Ribeira was Lisbon's waterfront where boats unloaded, goods were loaded and traded all day.
Fish was carried by water from Lisbon to Santarém.

lines.en: Here's the Ribeira. Loading and unloading all day, and everything bought and sold. From here the fish goes on by water to Santarém. My canoa is just one link.
lines.pt: Cá está a Ribeira. Cargas e descargas o dia todo, e tudo se compra e vende. Daqui o peixe segue pela água até Santarém. A minha canoa é só um elo.

claims.claim: Boats loaded and unloaded nonstop at the Ribeira
Some fish went by sea out of the kingdom
Some fish went by water to Santarém
Loading and unloading at the Ribeira went on constantly.
Fish was transported by sea out of the kingdom and by water from Lisbon to Santarém.

lines.en: Ribeira, at last. Boats loading and unloading nonstop. Some fish goes by sea out of the kingdom, some by water to Santarém. Tomorrow, another trip.
lines.pt: Ribeira, finalmente. Barcos a carregar e a descarregar sem parar. Há peixe que segue por mar para fora do Reino, outro pela água para Santarém. Amanhã, outra viagem.
